title: Reporters on the Job: From Paris to Salina, Kansas
text:
Paris – Colette Davidson
A reporter is never entirely off duty. News can happen anytime, even during a family walk in Paris.
Which is what I was doing when I came upon French anti-riot police blocking protesters from the central square known as Place de la République. Officers were throwing stun grenades and tear gas, pushing people back. When I tried filming, my press card visible, an officer told me to “get lost.” I retreated but kept recording, capturing an officer violently grabbing a middle-aged woman by the arm. Afterward, I sought her out to hear her account. As I recorded our interview on my phone, I realized I didn’t even have a pen with me. I had gone out for a walk with my family, not to report a story. But I was there, witnessing what happened, and I knew I needed to document it.
Kharkiv, Ukraine – Dominique Soguel
I’ve covered Ukraine since before Russia’s full-scale invasion, primarily with a translator’s help. But on a reporting trip in October, I could use my mother tongue, Spanish, to report on Colombians fighting in Ukraine. Thousands of Colombians have traveled to Ukraine, often serving in assault roles on the front lines, with most speaking little Ukrainian. The language barrier compounds the hardship when someone is killed or goes missing, leaving relatives struggling to get answers from a military thousands of miles away. Meeting Colombian soldiers and their families showed me a different Ukraine, a different war. It also revealed something universal: A Ukrainian mother’s grief and a Colombian mother’s might be expressed differently, but the pain needs no translation. At a Kharkiv memorial, two mothers shared photographs of their sons. They had no words in common yet understood each other perfectly. 
Kruger National Park, South Africa – Melanie Stetson Freeman
A photo I shot in 2002 of a bat in South Africa is running with our Endeavors profile in this week’s issue (“Building a bridge between bats and people,” page 28). It reminded me of the neat way I got the image. I was on a safari with a group that included a talented studio photographer who used a lot of lighting in his work. We saw this tiny bat hanging from the rafters outside a concession stand in Kruger National Park. He asked me to get a pillow from my room. What? Why? I wondered. He told me to hold it under the bat while he took his shot, then did the same for me. Turns out, the white pillowcase reflected light up onto the bat so there were highlights in its eyes. It was awesome to learn something new. 
Salina, Kansas – Sophie Hills
On the trail with Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate here, I found myself with time to spare before his campaign event at a Kansas bookstore. Linda Riedy, an attendee browsing the shelves, shared concerns common to other voters: a dysfunctional Congress, healthcare cuts, and the cost of living. But Ms. Riedy had a more personal connection: Mr. Hamilton is her cousin. Her great-grandparents were Mr. Hamilton’s great-great-grandparents, she explained, pulling out a binder complete with a family tree. They had never met, though they soon would. Like encounters in Ohio and Iowa, where I met voters who had been childhood neighbors or classmates of candidates, the conversation offered a glimpse of how politics can be deeply local – and how reporting on a campaign trail can reveal relationships and histories that a candidate’s stump speech never would.
